5hddovblvj51didavk6ajdjvj9.value: Credits: rotors as the way to turn things in any number of dimensions, and reflections as sandwiches, are David Hestenes' geometric algebra (New Foundations for Classical Mechanics, 1986), built on W. K. Clifford's algebras (1878) (prior art). Writing one physics step for 2D and 3D by changing only the algebra follows the geometric algebra teaching of Leo Dorst, Daniel Fontijne and Stephen Mann (Geometric Algebra for Computer Science, 2007) and Steven De Keninck's ganja.js and bivector.net examples (influence). The bodies, the step and the page are ours.

fgfpng9b4lhact351q6fadjsk9.value: Bounce: one physics step, two and three dimensions

adftuoi2q26up0uslrgn7meld3.value: The bodies on the left live in Cl(2, 0), the plane; those on the right in Cl(3, 0), space. Both are moved by the same definitions, step, moved, off the walls and bounced, given a different algebra: positions and velocities are vectors, turns are rotors, spins are bivectors, a wall reflects a velocity, and two bodies that meet trade the part of their velocities along the line between them (a projection).

fdhg0ir2mefgnmtfr1rde1j4op.value: Multivectors of 4 parts. One plane to spin in, e₁e₂.

3pfnrj2lgd3222gjfbomhjsupv.value: Multivectors of 8 parts. Each body spins in a plane of its own.

238h9hj9ac07sr5fqk6ftgdaph.value: A rotor R turns a corner c to R c R̃ (clifford sandwich). A spin Ω turns the body by e^(−dt/2 Ω) each frame (clifford exp), multiplied in front of R. In the plane Ω can only be a multiple of e₁e₂; in space it is any plane, and the same exp makes the rotor.

mbmmvlcv5bc3h6f55cdd4bcqn9.value: The flat world's algebra has 4 parts and the solid one's 8, and the tables that multiply them are built once from their signatures, [1, 1] and [1, 1, 1] (clifford algebra). The step never says which it has.
